Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

2611.17237.title: Permutation patterns and higher connectivity in inversion graphs
2611.17237.abstract: We prove that any permutation $π\in S_n$ whose inversion graph is $k$-connected has at least $\frac{k+1}{2}n - C$ inversions, where $C$ depends only on $k$. In particular, inversion graphs beat the general lower bound $\frac{kn}{2}$ for the number of edges in a $k$-connected graph. Furthermore, we characterize the permutation patterns $σ$ having the property that if $π$ avoids $σ$, then the bound improves to $kn - C$. The collection of patterns is $\mathrm{Av}(321, 2341, 4123)$, and it is independent of $k \geq 2$. This work is motivated by a result of Linusson and Verkama (2025) that can be reinterpreted as stating that any $1324$-avoiding permutation whose inversion graph satisfies a certain weaker notion of $2$-connectivity must have at least $2n - C$ inversions. Our final result gives a characterization of the patterns having this stronger property.

2611.17295.title: Traces of Vacuum Squeezing: A Superconducting Transmission-Line Analogue of Cosmological Particle Creation
2611.17295.abstract: Particle creation in time-dependent quantum fields is a central phenomenon in early-universe cosmology, yet it remains experimentally inaccessible in its original context. We show theoretically that superconducting circuits based on a waveguide-like transmission line loaded with dc-SQUIDs can provide a direct analogue of a scalar field in a radiation-dominated Friedmann--Robertson--Walker universe in conformal time. The mode equation of the circuit reduces to the Weber equation, the same equation governing cosmological particle creation in a radiation-dominated background, admitting an exact solution in terms of parabolic cylinder functions and an exponentially suppressed particle spectrum. We analyse the conditions under which the analogy holds, which require a compromise between the duration of the pulse, the uniformity of the modulation and the symmetry of the SQUIDs, and show that dissipation does not erase the cosmological signal. We use the anomalous moment of each mode as a witness of the Bogoliubov mixing: it vanishes for any thermal state and survives dissipation, and, together with the photon number, it certifies squeezing, and with the purity of the state, it identifies whether the pairs created from the vacuum dominate.

2611.17278.title: Active-space construction in single-fragment coupled-cluster embedding for chemical reactions
2611.17278.abstract: We benchmark single-fragment quantum embedding, in which electron correlation---at the level of coupled-cluster theory with single, double, and perturbative triple excitations [CCSD(T)]---is restricted to orbitals associated with a chosen molecular fragment, and the remaining orbitals are frozen at the Hartree-Fock level. We compare several methods for constructing fragment active spaces, and we test their performance on 60 organic reaction energies and three reaction profiles. A common fragment projection operator is used to relate several of the tested orbital constructions. Regional embedding, based on density matrix embedding theory, is shown to give accurate and robust performance when used for both the occupied and virtual active orbitals. For virtual orbitals, fragment-centered projected atomic orbitals and fragment natural orbitals (defined by eigenvectors of a fragment MP2 density matrix) also perform well, but the latter typically retains larger virtual spaces. Composite MP2 corrections yield the largest improvement: combined with fragment natural orbitals, they give average reaction energy errors below 0.3 kcal/mol relative to full-system CCSD(T), with all individual errors below 1 kcal/mol. Reaction profiles show that accurate endpoint energies can conceal substantial barrier errors, emphasizing the importance of approximating omitted correlation.

2611.17097.title: Broadcast, Don't Replicate: Eliminating Weight HBM in Datacenter LLM Serving
2611.17097.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference at datacenter scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth limits. Because model weights are read-only and identical across instances, conventional architectures that replicate these parameters across the local DRAM of tens of thousands of accelerators incur massive capital expenditures, significant static power dissipation, and redundant memory-fetch energy. A recent proposal to use optical fiber loops as delay-line memory alleviates these issues, but its recirculating loop must hold the whole model: loop length grows with model size, slack is fixed when the ring is built, and the layouts that serve modern Mixture of Experts (MoE) models efficiently do not fit in it. We propose Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM), an open-ended hierarchical Tap-and-Amplify fiber architecture that generalizes and replaces the optical ring paradigm. A centralized memory server continuously broadcasts weights to distributed inference nodes that passively tap the data stream using receive-only co-packaged optics, delivering parameters directly to compute units without intermediate buffering. To overcome the limitations of continuous weight streaming, we use dynamically-sized slack to accommodate large and variable context lengths. We show how removing the restrictions of the optical ring allows OBM to efficiently serve MoE models. Evaluated at a datacenter scale of 80,000 accelerators, OBM eliminates petabytes of HBM while being competitive or better in throughput and energy per token than an HBM-based system.

2611.16241.title: Stretched bilayer-cytoskeleton links hold echinocytes in a model splenic slit
2611.16241.abstract: Stored red blood cells become echinocytes, growing spicules before losing membrane; the spleen clears the resulting small, spherical cells. Whether spicules alone hinder splenic passage is unknown. Shape and area change together. In a two-component model whose shrinking cytoskeleton raises spicules, we drove a discocyte and stage I to III echinocytes of equal area and volume through a model splenic slit. The pressure drop needed to pass rose with stage; stage III echinocytes were held at 37 to 50 times the pressure drop that passed the discocyte. Bilayer-cytoskeleton links stretched near full extension held these cells; lengthening them about twofold released a held cell. Capillary-sized channels, as in our device, separated the stages far less. Of the shape classes in stored blood, the model held at high pressure drops only storage-induced microerythrocytes, which perfused human spleens clear most. Spicules, besides membrane loss, may decide which stored cells the spleen retains.
2611.16241.comment: 35 pages, 8 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Materials included (pages S1-S16, 6 figures, 1 table); Movies S1 to S3 are ancillary files. The first two authors contributed equally

2611.16057.title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
2611.16057.abstract: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.
2611.16057.comment: v1: main text (20 pp., 7 figs.) and supplementary materials (12 figures)

2611.17255.title: The lifting problem for Galois representations of global fields
2611.17255.abstract: We prove that all mod $2$ Galois representations of a global field lift modulo $4$. In contrast, for every odd prime $p$, we exhibit examples of global Galois representations modulo $p$ that do not lift modulo $p^2$. Our methods also allow us to prove liftability of generalized quaternion groups and hence to complete the classification of liftable finite groups initiated by Khare and Merkurjev.

2611.17112.title: Acoustically driven motion of single molecules at hBN surfaces
2611.17112.abstract: Developments in single-molecule imaging and sensing techniques have enabled direct observation of biomolecular dynamics at interfaces, which has important implications for the fields of membrane biophysics, nanofluidic sensing and transport. However, integrating active surface transport, localization and control over molecule motion remains challenging, limiting further progress in the realization of single-molecule devices. Here, we introduce an integrated surface acoustic wave (SAW)-hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) platform as a contactless actuation platform for directional transport of biomolecules over hBN surfaces. hBN provides an atomically flat surface on which DNA can be confined and still retain in-plane mobility, whereas SAW actuation enables active and guided transport without requiring specific electrical, dielectric or magnetic properties of the biomolecules. Trajectory- and jump-based analyses show that increasing the SAW power leads to higher displacement bias in the streaming direction, resulting in transport velocities along increasingly more linearized trajectories. We thus demonstrate that SAWs can induce tunable directional transport of DNA molecules confined on hBN surfaces, providing a new approach for the on-chip manipulation of biomolecules in nanofluidic systems. Our findings have important implications for the development of advanced single-molecule sequencing platforms and other technologies for biomolecular manipulation and analysis.

2611.17299.title: Simulation-Based Priors and BAO Shifts from the Lyman-$α$ Forest at the Field Level
2611.17299.abstract: We present an analytic forward model for the Lyman-alpha (Ly-alpha) forest flux field based on cubic-order large-scale structure perturbation theory (effective field theory) calculations. We validate our cubic model on two sets of hydrodynamic simulations spanning $2 \leq z \leq 4$: the small-volume CAMELS suite, which spans a wide range of cosmological and astrophysical parameters, and the large-volume, high-resolution Sherwood simulations. We find qualitatively similar results for both at the power-spectrum level. The perturbative model reproduces the three-dimensional flux power spectrum of the simulations to $\sim 5\%$ down to $k \simeq 1$-$1.5\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$, depending on the redshift. This improves compared to previous quadratic perturbative forward models by up to 40%. Exploiting cosmic-variance cancellation in the field-level approach, we carry out precision measurements of the Lyman-alpha forest bias parameters from the CAMELS simulation suite. We use these measurements to analytically predict the shifts in the Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO) scaling parameters induced by nonlinearities in the three-dimensional Lyman-alpha forest clustering as a function of cosmological parameters. We find sub-percent shifts in both the radial and transverse directions with a noticeable dependence on cosmology and redshift. Finally, from the field-level fits we construct simulation-based priors that can be used for cosmological analyses of the Lyman-alpha forest with the currently observing Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). In addition, our cubic model captures the connected four-point function (trispectrum) of the forest, which opens up novel opportunities for accurate covariance matrix estimation for DESI and its successor, DESI-II.

2611.16792.title: Systematic Evaluation of Training Data Generation Strategies for Machine Learning-Based Molecular and Materials Property Prediction
2611.16792.abstract: Machine-learning (ML) models for molecular and materials property prediction are often trained on large datasets curated through arbitrary or generic sampling strategies. Such approaches can lead to the over- or under-representation of regions of chemical and materials space that are most relevant to the prediction task. An important challenge is therefore how to efficiently curate training data to maximize predictive performance while minimising the number of labelled examples required. Here, we systematically compare training data acquisition strategies for molecular and materials property prediction, ranging from random sampling to various active learning approaches. We evaluate their performance across different model classes, representations, datasets, and target properties. Our results show that the effectiveness of data acquisition strategies depend strongly on the interplay between the model, dataset, and prediction task, although uncertainty-based sampling generally outperforms alternative strategies. Based on these findings, we derive guidelines for selecting data acquisition strategies under a given labelling budget.

2611.16773.title: Large Pockels Effect in Multiaxial Ferroelectrics Induced by Polarization Reorientation
2611.16773.abstract: Materials with large linear electro-optic (Pockels) effect have significant potential for fabricating energy-efficient photonic devices. Previous strategies have mostly relied on structural softness---associated with phase boundary, domain wall, or strain induced phase transition---to create large Pockels effect in ferroelectrics. In this Letter, we show that polarization reorientation in multiaxial ferroelectrics may create structural softness and thus induce large Pockels effect. By developing a phenomenological theory, we find that multiaxial ferroelectrics exhibit a hysteretic relationship between the azimuth angles of the polarization and the electric field, and a possible divergence of the linear electro-optic coefficient may occur at an appropriate polarization azimuth angle. This suggests a brand-new strategy for engineering large Pockels effect in multiaxial ferroelectrics. We perform first-principles simulations on several multiaxial ferroelectrics and predict that polarization reorientation can significantly enhance the electro-optic coefficients in monolayer SnSe and bulk KNbO$_3$. This validates the soundness of our strategy and emphasizes multiaxial ferroelectrics as promising platforms toward large Pockels effect.

2611.16924.title: Squeezed terahertz light from nonlinear diamagnetism in ultrastrongly coupled two-dimensional electrons
2611.16924.abstract: Two-dimensional electron gases in terahertz cavities are among the most mature platforms for ultrastrong light--matter coupling, yet their collective response is captured by the linear Hopfield model, which has an exact classical correspondence. We show that the intrinsic band nonparabolicity of the electrons, recently revealed through nonlinear diamagnetism, turns this system into a quantum Kerr oscillator that squeezes terahertz light. Using a non-rotating-wave theory with ultrastrong-coupling-consistent input--output, an ab initio cavity bath, and a self-consistent model of electron heating, we predict output squeezing of 1.8--2.4\,dB with present GaAs samples in weakly confined cavities with quality factors of order $10^2$, and up to $\approx9$\,dB with modest improvements in mobility or cavity frequency. Carrier heating sets limits through a material figure of merit, which yields a simple design rule that the optimal cavity quality factor scales inversely with the ultrastrong-coupling strength.

2611.16881.title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
2611.16881.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. Across multiple architectures (ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) and model scales (8M to 3B parameters), pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. Using Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions, we attempt to isolate what likely causes this degradation and find that these models rely on explicit, canonical residue identities (``alphabet anchoring'') rather than pure coevolutionary statistics. Increasing scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but their performance still degrades under relabeling. Our findings show a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts. More broadly, our work shows how diagnostic perturbations that leave classical models provably unchanged can expose hidden representation biases and prevent over-reliance on neural black boxes in biological modeling.
2611.16881.comment: Accepted to the ICBINB - Failure Modes of AI in Biology Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 15 pages, 6 figures

2611.17277.title: On $L^p$ density of self-similar measures and Bernoulli convolutions
2611.17277.abstract: We prove that an absolutely continuous self-similar measure has an $L^p$ density for some $p>1$. Moreover, explicit examples of Bernoulli convolutions with a continuous density are established.

2611.17333.title: Discrete Time Crystals from Anti-Unitary Floquet Driving and Dynamical Freezing
2611.17333.abstract: We show anti-unitary periodic drive paves a direct path for stabilizing a Discrete Time-Crystal by Dynamical Freezing (DF). The magnetization appears as an emergent conserved operator, and an exact pairing of two-cycle quasi-energies pins the subharmonic response. DF keeps the effective Hamiltonian $\textit{quasi-local}$; infinite-chain simulations show no detectable decay for a generic state with any finite magnetization. We outline an experimental realization of the anti-unitary drive.

2611.17885.title: Goodman-type lower bounds for graph homomorphism densities
2611.17885.abstract: For a finite graph $H$ with $v(H)$ vertices, chromatic number $χ(H)$, and chromatic polynomial $P_H$, define $Φ_H(p)=(1-p)^{v(H)}P_H((1-p)^{-1})$. This polynomial interpolates the homomorphism densities of $H$ in balanced complete multipartite graphons. We study the lower bound $t(H,W)\geΦ_H(p)$ on the homomorphism density of $H$ in graphons $W$ of edge density $p>1-1/(χ(H)-1)$, which generalises Goodman's triangle bound. We prove the inequality for chordal graphs whose maximal cliques have equal size, for trivially perfect graphs, and for joins of a clique and an odd cycle. The proofs use entropy along clique trees and a convexity criterion for adding a universal vertex. We also prove that a nonbipartite graph satisfies the inequality at all sufficiently high edge densities if and only if its girth is odd. For a graph on $n$ vertices whose girth is odd, the bound holds whenever $p>1-(72n^{12})^{-1}$. The proof combines Whitney's forest expansion with a spectral comparison of cycle densities. Finally, among the $117$ nonbipartite graphs on at most six vertices with no isolated vertices or isolated edges, exactly $94$ satisfy the bound. The main results are formally verified in Lean 4.

2611.17855.title: On configurations that are nearly generalised polygons
2611.17855.abstract: Payne (1972) introduced nearly generalised $n$-gons as $(s+1)$-regular bipartite graphs of girth $2n$ with small excess over the Moore bound. Biggs and Ito (1980) proved nonexistence of such graphs if $s > 1$ and $n > 3$, leaving open the existence of regular antipodal planes. We revisit this problem from several equivalent viewpoints. First we show that a regular antipodal plane of order $s$ is equivalent to a balanced weighing matrix whose support is the incidence matrix of a biplane with parameters \[ 2-\left(\frac{s^2+s+2}{2},\,s+1,\,2\right). \] This gives short determinant and local-arithmetic obstructions to existence. We then formulate the question of signing a biplane as an affine linear system over $\mathbb F_2$, and use this formulation to prove that no regular antipodal plane of order $s$ exists with $4\le s\le 14$. Finally, we give further equivalent formulations in terms of sharply deranged families of permutations and mutually orthogonal array-bic squares. These translations provide new computational and structural approaches to Payne's conjecture that regular antipodal planes exist only for $s=2,3$.

2611.17842.title: Hardware-aware sampling and QPU-informed Monte Carlo with quantum annealers
2611.17842.abstract: We study how the physical representation of a logical model affects sampling by quantum annealers and its use in corrected Monte Carlo. The square-lattice Ising model provides controlled classical references. Fixed embeddings with one physical qubit per logical spin reach $36\times36$ spins. Comparisons with uniform two-qubit chains and mixed chain lengths show that matching mean energy leaves differences in magnetization and correlations. Extended-range conditional predictors improve the description of mixed embeddings, distinguishing their residual correlations from those of the tested uniform embeddings. Independent calibration checks and fixed-scale annealing scans show that temperature shifts alone do not determine distributional agreement. Normalized autoregressive models learned from QPU samples provide proposals with exact Metropolis--Hastings and multiple-try corrections on larger periodic lattices. These preserve the target distribution, although block updates alone relax critical magnetization slowly. Complementary direct-QPU updates reveal how block size and fitted-temperature correction affect acceptance and spin motion. Together, the results support prioritizing one-qubit representations and short uniform chains, while separating hardware sampling fidelity from the convergence of corrected Monte Carlo.

2611.17731.title: Ultrafast Imaging Reveals Energy Transport Anisotropy Grows from Bulk to Monolayer Black Phosphorus
2611.17731.abstract: Black phosphorus is an emerging low-dimensional semiconductor whose tunable band gap, high carrier mobility, and anisotropic transport make it attractive for directional energy transport in electronics and thermoelectrics. Using ultrafast stroboscopic optical scattering microscopy (stroboSCAT), we image spatiotemporal evolution of energy carriers with picosecond resolution, simultaneously resolving heat and charge transport in bulk black phosphorus and exciton transport in the monolayer. The in-plane armchair:zigzag anisotropy increases from 5.3:1 in the bulk to 6.7:1 in the monolayer, driven by enhanced armchair exciton diffusivity (45.5 cm$^2$/s) relative to bulk armchair charge carriers (16.5 cm$^2$/s). The monolayer anisotropy is smaller than the calculated exciton dispersion alone would suggest, which first-principles calculations attribute to preferential exciton-phonon scattering to large momenta along the zigzag direction. These directly measured, layer-resolved diffusivities identify armchair-aligned monolayers as the optimal geometry for directional transport and show that transport anisotropy cannot be inferred from band dispersion alone.

2611.17882.title: Quantum Fluctuations drive Emerging Bosonic Quantum Phases in a Moiré Flatband Superconductor
2611.17882.abstract: Quantum fluctuations play a central role in superconductors by mediating the interactions that promote electron pairing and controlling the phase coherence required for macroscopic condensation. Thus far, understanding the interplay between quantum fluctuations and superconductivity remains challenging in unconventional superconductors. Here, we establish quantum phase fluctuations as the organizing principle linking superconductivity and Bose-insulating quantum criticality in a moiré flatband superconductor of alternating twisted trilayer graphene (ATTG). Superconductivity is optimal near half-filling of the moiré flatband and gives way to a density-wave-like resistance peak at high temperatures, in which we observe distinct temperature scales for the pairing (~6 K) and the condensation (~1 K). We observe compelling evidence of a bosonic superconducting quantum phase transition, driven by both out-of-plane and in-plane magnetic fields, with a universal critical resistivity of $R_c =~0.62R_Q$ and finite-temperature scaling of $zν_B = 2.3$, where $R_Q = h/4e^2$ is the quantum resistance for bosons. Strikingly, the observed bosonic insulator shows a nearly quantized resistivity of $R_Q$ that saturates at low temperatures and high magnetic fields, together with a zero-bias peak, a nearly zero Hall resistance, and a logarithmic dependence at higher temperatures. Both the superconductor and the bosonic insulator could be driven into the same critical quantum fluctuation regime dynamically under a large bias. Our results establish moiré flatband as a clean platform for studying unconventional superconductivity and bosonic quantum criticality governed by quantum fluctuations.

2611.17833.title: Probing the Activity History of Repeating Fast Radio Bursts with Cluster Lensing
2611.17833.abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond duration coherent radio transients, some of whose sources repeat, but the nature and active lifetimes of their engines remain uncertain. Strong lensing by galaxy clusters provides a physical lever on this lifetime problem: a short campaign can sample emission epochs of a repeating FRB separated by years, and distinct bursts in different lensed images, given a known relative lens delay, set a lower bound on its active lifetime, whereas delayed copies of a single burst only encode the lens delay. Based on the cluster-lens model of MACS J0717.5+3745, we quantify the accessible range of emission epochs for finite activity episodes, observing windows, and discovery selection. For a source-frame episode of duration \(100~{\rm yr}\) at \(z_s=2\) and a source-frame rate of \(0.1\,{\rm h}_{\rm src}^{-1}\), a five year campaign conditional on discovery yields a \(95\%\) gain threshold of \(m_{95}\simeq25.6\), corresponding to a source-frame span of \(L_{95}\simeq42.6~{\rm yr}\). At the population level, combining distinct burst associations with same burst echoes provides a way to test specified activity durations with a finite lens catalogue, e.g., activity durations differing by an order of magnitude can be distinguished with expected Bayes factor above $20$. More broadly, these lensed source frame epochs enable applications beyond activity-duration tests, e.g., linking burst activity to the evolution of the engine and its environment. Galaxy-cluster lensing therefore provides a promising future probe for accessing otherwise unobserved source history and for distinguishing between different activity duration models.

2611.17723.title: uhd-rfsoc: Bringing Off-the-Shelf RFSoC Boards to Unmodified UHD Applications
2611.17723.abstract: Next-generation wireless research relies on software-defined radios (SDRs) with more channels and larger bandwidth. The USRP family is one of the most widely used SDR platforms, and much of the wireless software ecosystem is built on top of the USRP hardware driver (UHD). However, each USRP model comes with a fixed channel count, bandwidth, and streaming capability. Off-the-shelf radio frequency system-on-chip (RFSoC) boards, on the other hand, integrate up to 16 analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) and 16 digital-to-analog converters (DACs) operating at several gigasamples per second (GS/s), but existing UHD applications cannot directly use them. We present uhd-rfsoc, an open-source FPGA design and host software stack that turns these boards, including the 16-channel ZCU216 and the RFSoC 4x2, into standard UHD devices without modifying UHD. Through standard UHD calls, applications can configure the carrier frequency, channel count, the per-channel I/Q sample rate, and the wire format. uhd-rfsoc combines timestamped, flow-controlled sample transport in the FPGA with data plane development kit (DPDK) packet processing and vectorized sample conversion on x86 and Arm hosts. The built bitstreams for a number of RFSoC board configurations with varying RF data converter rates, channel counts, I/Q sample rates, and wire formats all successfully pass UHD's built-in streaming benchmarks. We further demonstrate compatibility with unmodified GNU Radio flowgraphs, a custom GPU-accelerated transceiver digital signal processing pipeline, as well as the OCUDU and Duranta 5G radio access network stacks using both software and commodity user equipment.

2611.17741.title: Vision-Language Models Reproduce a Human Mental-Extrapolation Bias in the Watanabe Illusion
2611.17741.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for visual judgments, yet whether they share human perceptual biases, and where in the model such biases arise, is unclear. We addressed this with the Watanabe Illusion, a stimulus not previously studied quantitatively: an oblique segment inside a circle whose extension geometrically hits the topmost of 11 dots, yet human observers (n = 131) reported a dot near the middle of the column. Five VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-32B and 7B, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.5 Instant, Gemini 3.5 Flash), given the identical stimulus and wording, all deviated in the same direction. In the open-weight Qwen2.5-VL-32B, linear probes on the vision encoder recovered the line angle and the target dot six to eight times more accurately than its behavioral responses. A layer-wise logit lens showed that the correct answer dominates in the middle layers of the language model and is overwritten in late layers only under a visual-judgment frame. Naming the illusion, requesting suppression of prior knowledge, forcing a visual chain of thought, and 390 semantic preambles left the response center unchanged; only disclosing the correct answer moved it. VLMs may therefore carry human perceptual biases at the language-generation stage, where they resist declarative correction.
2611.17741.comment: 44 pages, 4 figures, 4 appendices. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23096369

2611.17615.title: Data-driven exploration of the strength-ductility synergy in refractory high-entropy alloys
2611.17615.abstract: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have attracted increasing attention for their exceptional ability to retain strength at high temperatures. However, current research mainly concentrates on compositions close to equimolar alloys, leaving a large part of the composition space unexplored. Here, we develop a multiscale framework based on a data-driven dislocation genome method that constructs energy landscapes for edge dislocation motion across various compositions. The local configurational force derived from the energy landscape is incorporated into dislocation dynamics simulations, revealing a scaling law connecting macroscale strength and atomic-scale local resistance governed by fluctuations in the local configurational force. Based on this scaling law, a new solid-solution strengthening model for edge dislocation in BCC alloys is developed, followed by a data-driven exploration of refractory alloys considering both strength and ductility. The developed method and theory are adaptable, allowing for extension to other BCC alloy systems and guiding high-throughput alloy design.

2611.17795.title: Striatal Optogenetic Modulation Shifts Seizure Onset Timing: A Survival-Analysis Reanalysis with Effect Sizes, Permutation Validation, and Sensitivity Analysis
2611.17795.abstract: We present a worked methods vignette, not a novel biological claim: a reanalysis of the public dataset accompanying Hyder and colleagues' report that optogenetic activation and inhibition of the dorsal striatum bidirectionally control seizures, applying a time-to-event framework to the pilocarpine-induced status epilepticus (SE) arm, the only arm with genuine per-animal event-level data rather than aggregate statistics. The original study compared latencies with a Mann-Whitney U test (ChR2 vs GFP: p = 0.0125; ArchT vs GFP: p = 0.0025). We first directly replicate that test on the same data (p = 0.0151 and p = 0.0025), confirming we analyze the same numbers, then designate the log-rank test as this reanalysis's pre-specified primary comparison, with a Cox model, a label-permutation test, a bootstrap confidence interval, and a leave-one-out analysis serving as validation checks rather than co-equal findings. ChR2 activation delays SE onset relative to its paired GFP control (hazard ratio 0.338, 95% CI 0.128-0.895; log-rank p = 0.023), and ArchT inhibition accelerates it (hazard ratio 9.18, 95% CI 1.91-44.09; log-rank p = 0.0011); a Schoenfeld-residual check found no significant proportional-hazards violation, though this check has limited power at n = 8-11 per group. Both results are confirmed by a 2,000-shuffle permutation test and survive leave-one-out, though the ChR2 comparison loses significance in 2 of 20 leave-one-out iterations, a fragility we report rather than omit. We do not claim this demonstrates anything the field did not already believe; its value is methodological, a reusable survival-analysis template with a Cox-derived effect size and documented sensitivity, extending naturally to future datasets with genuine censoring, which this one does not have.

2611.17698.title: Pressure-driven evolution of crystal and molecular structures reshapes excited-state competition in coronene
2611.17698.abstract: Molecular nanocarbons exhibit unique optoelectronic properties and considered as promising candidates for organic device applications, however, understanding how molecular geometry and crystal packing jointly govern physical properties remains a fundamental challenge in π-conjugated molecular materials. Here, we demonstrate how these structural factors modulate the photoluminescence of coronene under high pressure. Combining high-pressure single-crystal X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, optical spectroscopy, and density functional theory calculations, we establish a relationship between distinct structural changes and the evolution of competing emissive states. Our results reveal that crystal polymorphism modifies the balance between free-exciton (FE) and self-trapped-exciton (STE) emission, while pressure-induced molecular bending is associated with a nonmonotonic evolution of STE emission. As intermolecular distances shorten, enhanced intermolecular electronic interactions give rise to excimer-related emission, introducing an additional emissive pathway. Although pressure-dependent optical properties of coronene have been linked to changes in crystal packing, our findings highlight that the optical response of a molecular solid is not governed by molecular deformation or crystal packing alone, but emerges from their interplay with intermolecular electronic coupling. By directly resolving molecular bending alongside changes in excited-state emission, this work provides insight into how distinct structural degrees of freedom can reshape the photophysical behavior of π-conjugated molecular solids.

2611.17532.title: Astrocyte Biocomputing: Astrocytic Contributions to Neural Network Computation
2611.17532.abstract: Conductors are critical for the performance of an orchestra even though they do not emit sound. Basic research and clinical studies in the last decade are revealing that astrocytes may be the "conductors" of the "orchestra" that is the brain network: astrocytes make up approximately $50\%$ of all brain cells but do not emit electrical signals. Nevertheless, they may play critical roles in important cognitive brain functions, specifically learning, memory, and information processing. Here we consider the implications of these discoveries for brain-inspired machine learning (ML), where analogy is typically drawn between neurons and their electrical interactions. We highlight specific algorithms for two key astrocyte characteristics. The first characteristic is the ability to link to and modulate thousands of synapses simultaneously. A model based on this characteristic yields faster training and makes the network more robust to noise, providing a supervised learning algorithm that can be applied to any existing neural network. The second characteristic we focus on is that the non-electrical communication among astrocytes includes slow, rhythmic dynamics. The rhythmic sharing algorithm we developed based on this premise yields rapid anomaly detection adaptation and prevents catastrophic forgetting. Overall, we find that astrocyte-derived algorithms outperform neurocentric algorithms significantly and remediate critical weaknesses of current state-of-the-art ML models.

2611.17844.title: A Helly theorem for the Bruhat-Tits building
2611.17844.abstract: Let $K$ be a discretely valued field with valuation ring $\mathcal{O}$. We show that a finite family of $\mathcal{O}$-lattices in $K^m$ is adapted to a common basis if any subfamily of at most $m+1$ $\mathcal{O}$-lattices is. In other words, in the Bruhat-Tits building of $\operatorname{GL}(m)$, a finite family of simplices lies in a common apartment if and only if any subfamily of at most $m+1$ simplices does. The proof uses a version of Radon's theorem for $\mathcal{O}$-lattices. We also give an alternative proof using truncated modules.

2611.17679.title: Electric Fields Turn Vacancy-trapping Grain Boundaries into Li-Ion Pathways in Li2O
2611.17679.abstract: Ion transport in solids has conventionally been understood from equilibrium diffusion, yet ions in batteries are driven by electric fields. Does field-driven ion transport follow equilibrium behavior? We examined this question in bulk Li2O and at its grain boundaries (GBs) using electric-field molecular dynamics combining a machine learning interatomic potential with a Bader charge prediction model. Although Li diffusion in cubic Li2O is isotropic at zero field, an electric field renders it orientation dependent because Li hops along a limited set of crystallographic pathways that the field biases unequally. At GBs, this anisotropy becomes a qualitative difference: a GB that strongly traps Li vacancies but exhibits a strong field response releases them under a field, whereas a weakly responsive GB retains them despite weaker vacancy trapping. These results show that field-driven GB transport is governed not by static thermodynamics alone but by the angle between the electric field and the diffusion pathways of the constituent grains.

2611.17634.title: A Unified Device-Level Physical Framework for DRAM Read Disturbance
2611.17634.abstract: Read disturbance in dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) depends on both local device interactions and the electrical conditions imposed by shared array circuitry. Here, we combine DIMM-level characterization results, device measurements, and TCAD simulations to interpret RowHammer, RowPress, and ColumnDisturb within a unified device-level physical framework. We relate charge evolution at the floating storage node to three key mechanisms: trap-assisted electron migration (EM), capacitive coupling (CC), and sense-amplifier-mediated disturb (SAMD). EM is local and trap-sensitive, while CC weakens with wordline separation. SAMD extends disturbance through shared column circuitry by modifying unselected-cell leakage under rail-level bitline biases, a contribution supported by the approximately ninefold higher OFF-state leakage measured relative to retention-like conditions for a high-voltage storage state. These distinct spatial ranges account for localized RowHammer and RowPress failures and remote ColumnDisturb populations with abrupt changes at subarray boundaries. We further interpret prolonged RowPress activation as a transition from an initial RowHammer-like transient to sustained leakage driven mainly by SAMD under held wordline and bitline biases. Within this device-level framework, trap effectiveness and storage-state-dependent leakage provide an interpretation of previously puzzling failure signatures, including the earlier onset of 0-to-1 RowHammer failures despite the predominance of 1-to-0 failures at high hammer counts. The same framework explains the observed RowPress and ColumnDisturb polarities and the duration-dependent reversal of neighboring- and passing-wordline effectiveness. These results provide a physical basis for developing compact DRAM reliability models across access patterns and array configurations.

2611.19339.title: From Mutation to Medication: Characterizing Failures of Clinical LLMs to Respect Genomic Resistance
2611.19339.abstract: Language models are increasingly proposed to support molecular tumour boards, but may recommend cancer therapies despite genomic evidence of resistance. We evaluated ten models on 1,464 resistance cases from five curated oncology knowledge bases, collecting 58,910 judgments. Models endorsed resisted therapies in 21.8-81.4% of cases. However, raw rates can reflect a tendency to agree rather than an ability to distinguish resistance from drug sensitivity: one open-weight model endorsed 81.4% of resistance cases and 82.3% of sensitivity controls. We therefore compared endorsement within matched gene and evidence-level groups. This analysis is exploratory because it was specified after the pre-registered analysis, which yielded null-to-weak results. Measured failures depended strongly on the reference knowledge base and evidence strength. When a second source independently confirmed resistance, four models across three vendors endorsed at most 2.4% of cases; at weaker evidence tiers, discrimination was not measurable. Models sometimes acknowledged resistance yet recommended the therapy. Repeating a model's own resistance conclusion reduced endorsement to 0.0-3.5% on cases where it had stated resistance. Falsely attributing the opposite conclusion increased endorsement above baseline for all seven hosted models, reaching 95.2% for GPT-4o; an instruction without an attributed conclusion changed endorsement by only 0.9 percentage points. Providing the correct curated evidence reduced unqualified strong recommendations to 0.3-3.5%, testing evidence use under an oracle condition rather than retrieval.
2611.19339.comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026 Symposium

2611.19257.title: A unified cross-scale framework for the dynamic Waddington landscape
2611.19257.abstract: The Waddington epigenetic landscape is a foundational concept in developmental biology, yet its quantitative formulations remain largely disconnected from the population dynamics that originally motivated the metaphor. Existing approaches typically describe either intracellular gene-regulatory dynamics or population-level cell kinetics, but rarely both within a unified framework. Here, we develop a unified PDE-integral framework that couples stochastic gene-regulatory dynamics with probability-conserving population renewal, yielding a dynamic Waddington landscape $U(\vec{x}, t) = -\log f(\vec{x}, t)$ defined directly from the evolving epigenetic probability density $f(\vec{x}, t)$. Rigorous mathematical analysis of this framework establishes its well-posedness and provides conditions for the existence and uniqueness of stationary solutions. Application to canonical gene regulatory circuits shows that proliferation is not merely a determinant of population size, but an active regulator of landscape topology. Population renewal reshapes attractor stability and transition barriers in a circuit-dependent manner, generating transient plasticity in some regulatory architectures while stabilizing progenitor states in others. Under highly proliferative conditions, these interactions further produce oscillatory ``breathing'' landscapes. Together, these results establish population renewal as an integral component of cell-fate regulation and extend the Waddington landscape from a static description of intracellular dynamics to a predictive multiscale framework linking gene regulation, cell-state dynamics, and tissue homeostasis.

2611.20138.title: Planar PArcK is PSPACE-complete
2611.20138.abstract: Partizan Arc Kayles, or PArcK, is a partizan combinatorial game on edge colored graphs, and is a generalization of the game Domineering. Previously, PArcK was shown to be PSPACE-complete on bipartite graphs. In this paper we show that PArcK is PSPACE-complete even when restricted to planar graphs of degree at most three by a reduction from Generalized Hex.

2611.20121.title: Matching two-dimensional statistics does not certify three-dimensional transport in battery electrodes
2611.20121.abstract: Three-dimensional battery electrode structures reconstructed from two-dimensional micrographs are routinely used to predict transport, assuming that matching the measured 2D statistics reproduces the relevant 3D properties. We test this premise on X-ray tomograms of three all-solid-state cathodes. With a differentiable conductivity solver, we optimise voxel structures that match the real electrode in phase fractions, boundary density, two- and three-point correlations and lineal-path functions, on all section planes, slab by slab and layer by layer, within measurement noise. Every sample has statistical twins conducting 10-88-fold less than the real electrode, robust to 5^3 majority filtering, whereas the most conductive are at most 3.3-fold above it. The twins rearrange rather than remove material, severing or funnelling through-plane paths. A classifier on 2D sections detects them, as it does current 2D-to-3D generators: the information is in the images but not in the statistics. Matching standard 2D statistics therefore does not certify 3D transport.
2611.20121.comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables; includes Supplementary Information

2611.18561.title: FETTUCCINE: Fast and efficient brain-to-text decoding on mobile devices
2611.18561.abstract: Recent advances in speech neuroprostheses have enabled new communication avenues for people who have lost the ability to speak due to neurological illness or injury. These systems can decode neural activity during attempted speech into text by relying on language priors to achieve high decoding accuracy. This performance currently comes at the cost of using a compute-intensive language modeling stack, presenting a major bottleneck for real-world use. Further, current language models incur highly variable and disruptive inference latencies, limiting communication throughput and preventing users from reliably participating in natural conversation. We introduce FETTUCCINE, an end-to-end brain-to-text framework that leverages the speed and portability of automatic speech recognition (ASR) models to address the aforementioned practical challenges, while achieving usable (<10%) word error rates (WER), efficient adaptation to neural non-stationarities, and reliable performance on mobile devices. When evaluated using publicly available data from an intracortical speech neuroprosthesis user, FETTUCCINE outperforms previous end-to-end methods, achieving as low as 4.39% WER. Most notably, our models successfully run on a commercially-available mobile device with throughput reaching up to 370x real-time, providing the first demonstration of brain-to-text decoding on a mobile device. We also show that our models can be successfully finetuned to extend usable performance to future days. Beyond performance, our approach enables localization of the neural features most relevant for decoding via gradient-based saliency maps, which we show align with well-established physiological priors across different ASR model families. Taken together, our results show that FETTUCCINE overcomes core infrastructural and computational barriers, yielding a new class of portable brain-to-text communication.

2611.19915.title: CHERI under Fault Injection: An Emulation-Based Security Evaluation of Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions
2611.19915.abstract: Memory-safety vulnerabilities continue to dominate real-world exploit chains despite decades of research into software mitigations. CHERI is a hardware architecture that enforces spatial and temporal memory safety by augmenting pointers with hardware-checked metadata, thus preventing software-based exploitation, but its threat model explicitly excludes fault injection. This thesis investigates whether targeted fault injection can undermine CHERI's memory-safety guarantees in a pure-capability CHERI-RISC-V environment. Two fault classes are considered: bit flips corrupting capability metadata, and fault-induced check skipping on capability store instructions. We implement fault injection primitives in a QEMU-based emulation environment, which enables deterministic, repeatable experiments without specialised hardware. With them, we demonstrate four attack scenarios: buffer overflows, control-flow hijacking, data-only attacks, and use-after-free. Each succeeds with one or two targeted faults (lower bounds under the emulation-based setting). Check skipping offers an alternative route to control-flow hijacking and data-only attacks, with a minimum of one fault. These results show that CHERI's guarantees depend on the physical integrity of capability metadata, the uninterrupted execution of metadata checks, and the integrity of the revocation bitmap: a single targeted fault can circumvent spatial safety, temporal safety, or control-flow integrity. CHERI still raises the cost of exploitation, since fault injection is a prerequisite for every attack and the sentry mechanism forces an attacker to supply a valid tagged capability or spend a second fault restoring the tag. Based on these findings, we propose mitigations: ECC-protected capability memory, capability field authentication codes, redundant execution of security-critical checks, and revocation bitmap integrity verification.
2611.19915.comment: Submitted to KTH Royal Institute on Technology as a Master Thesis

2611.20170.title: Stabilization of LaH$_{10}$ with Thorium: Superconductivity in (La,Th)H$_{10}$ up to 232 K near 1 Mbar
2611.20170.abstract: Ternary lanthanum-based hydrides are among the best high-temperature superconductors. Here we show that substituting La with thorium stabilizes La(Th)H$_{10}$ clathrate structure at $\sim$1 Mbar while only minimally suppressing superconductivity. The resulting cubic (La,Th)H$_{10}$ phase, synthesized from relatively air-stable La$_2$Th, La$_3$Th and La$_5$Th alloys, reaches an onset $\textit{T$_c$}$ = 232 K at 134 GPa, as confirmed by contact resistance measurements. Superconductivity was verified by two independent methods: electrical resistance and contactless radio-frequency measurements under applied magnetic fields at various pressures. Using a record-high pulsed current of 380 mA, we investigated critical phenomena in P6$_3$/mmc-(La,Th)H$_9$ at 173 GPa, which allowed for the experimental determination of a single superconducting gap within the s-wave model: $Δ(0) = 37 \pm 4.5$ meV and $2Δ(0)/kT_c = 4.9 \pm 0.6$. The La-Th-H system is chemically rich: in addition to the decahydride and nonahydride mentioned above, we also identified nanocrystalline I4/mmm-(La,Th)H$_4$ (5-6 nm grain size), (La,Th)H$_6$, as well as $hP13$, $cF80$ and $A15$ phases with compositions of (La,Th)H$_{5.75-6.25}$ and $\textit{T$_c$}$ $\approx$ 83 K at 70-80 GPa, and a possible (La,Th)H$_{16}$ polyhydride.

2611.20118.title: A Forward Bit Makes Error Correction Dispensable for Antidegradable Amplitude-Damping Channels
2611.20118.abstract: Preserving a qubit usually relies on redundant encoding over many uses of a noisy channel. We prove that for antidegradable amplitude damping, one channel use with one forward classical bit matches or beats every forward-assisted or unassisted code with any number of uses. We then show that variational circuits learn to switch from error correction to classical assistance as damping grows, beating a dual-certified bound on all unassisted three-use codes and, relative to the best unassisted see-saw, extending storage time by up to 13% at entanglement fidelity down to 0.65.

2611.20047.title: CleanRoute: Reconciling DRC Compliance, Post-Layout Performance, and Runtime in Analog Routing
2611.20047.abstract: Automated analog routing remains a long-standing challenge because design-rule checking (DRC) compliance, post-layout performance preservation, and runtime reduction are difficult to achieve together. Existing analog routers have limited coverage of joined-metal design rules, lack control over topology-induced mismatch, and face a trade-off between DRC violations and runtime on uniform routing grids. In this paper, we introduce CleanRoute, an analog router that reconciles these three targets. Hierarchical rule enforcement assigns DRC checks and repairs to stages where the required geometry is complete, covering rules both between separate metal and where metal joins. IR-drop isolation constructs supply trees from current-mirror relationships and device currents to reduce topology-induced mismatch that geometric matching cannot eliminate and voltage drops along high-current paths. A flush-line grid adds net-specific lines aligned with device-metal edges to a coarse routing grid, providing DRC-compliant connections without uniform refinement. Experiments on ten operational transconductance amplifiers (OTAs) in a commercial 40nm process show that CleanRoute produces DRC-clean and functional layouts that pass layout versus schematic (LVS) checking on all benchmarks, with the strongest overall performance preservation and a median routing runtime of 8.82s, whereas the baselines produce no DRC-clean layouts.

2611.20194.title: Quantum-Enhanced Passive and Active Radio-Frequency Photonic Imaging
2611.20194.abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) photonics enables broadband, phase-coherent sensing beyond the reach of purely electronic architectures, yet at a given optical carrier power its sensitivity is bounded by the standard quantum limit of the optical readout. Here, we experimentally demonstrate that this limit can be surpassed in both passive and active RF imaging modalities by encoding RF signals onto a bright phase-squeezed optical carrier and recovering them via balanced homodyne detection, while the RF front end, illumination, and image reconstruction remain classical. A unified measurement model shows that phase squeezing reduces the variance of the additive readout noise by a single factor $g$, yielding peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) gains of up to $2G$, where $G\equiv10\log_{10}(1/g)$: between $G$ and $2G$ for deterministic targets in active imaging when the classical noise of the echoes is negligible against the readout noise, and set by the ratio of scene noise to readout noise in passive imaging. We validate the model in an experiment in the 5--20 MHz band, in which synthesized RF scenes are replayed through a physical squeezed-light receiver. With 3 dB of squeezing, the PSNR improves by about 6 dB, close to $2G$, in the readout-noise-dominated regime of both modalities, and the model predicts the measured gains without free parameters. These results identify where squeezed-light readout benefits RF-photonic imaging: wherever the optical readout noise, rather than the scene or the RF front end, dominates the image error.

2611.20022.title: The microscopic origin of the hysteretic hydrogen adsorption in Double Wall Carbon Nanotubes bundles
2611.20022.abstract: In a recent study we reported large hysteretic hydrogen adsorption in samples made out of Double Wall Carbon Nanotubes (DWCNT) at supercritical temperatures (50 K, 77 K and 150 K), a physical behavior of practical interest. Here, we center our efforts in elucidate its physical origin by means of neutron diffraction (ND) and computer simulations. After a detailed theoretical modeling of the ND signal we were able to quantitatively study how the nanostructure of the material reacts to the hydrogen loads. An expansion of the bundle structure with increasing hydrogen load was found. Taking advantage of the translational symmetry of a DWCNT bundle along the nanotube axis, a two dimensional numerical analogue of the system helped us to clarify the microscopic origin of the hysteresis. Two microscopic mechanisms are identified as responsible for the metastable hydrogen adsorption, one structurally static in character, namely, H$_{2}$-load dependent effective energy barriers between interstitials, the other related to the structural deformation, namely, the opening/closing of the channels between interstitials with increasing/decreasing H$_{2}$ loads owing to the concomitant bundle expansion/contraction.

2611.19931.title: Does synthetic pre-training pay off on a microcontroller? Accuracy, latency and energy across two MCUs
2611.19931.abstract: Rendered images are cheap to label, but a microcontroller classifier must survive 8-bit integer (INT8) quantisation and compute correctly on the chip. Five models, from MobileNetV2 at 224 px to a 61K-parameter convolutional neural network (CNN), were fine-tuned on a six-class scene dataset with and without a synthetic stage, against thresholds fixed in advance, and deployed on an ESP32-S3 and an RP2040. With full real data the stage gave no detectable gain. For the main deployable model the INT8 difference was +0.312 percentage points (pp), its interval below the +1.6 pp gain recomputed from the source study; quantisation did not detectably change it, nor did model size. With 10% of the real data the stage paid off for the CNN, by +3.438 pp on one seed and +2.715 pp over three; its cause is open. On the ESP32-S3 the main model took 152.7 ms and 16.3 mJ above idle per inference, and adding the stage changed neither beyond preset bounds. The model's INT8 outputs matched TensorFlow Lite's reference kernels exactly, but only after a memory overrun in a vendor kernel was patched. On the RP2040 the same model took 1.80 s and 27.3 mJ above idle, about twelve times slower, and the largest 96 px model exceeded the board's flash-capacity limit. Neither the RP2040 nor the host interpreter used for scoring reproduced the reference arithmetic. A synthetic stage is worth adding only when real data are scarce, and on-device INT8 outputs should be checked against reference kernels, not inferred from host scores.
2611.19931.comment: 43 pages, 5 figures, 14 tables; supplementary tables, figures and notes as ancillary files. Analysis plan registered on OSF (doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/BPQGA). Under review

2611.20205.title: Independent set reconfiguration is hard at treewidth four
2611.20205.abstract: Independent Set Reconfiguration asks whether one of two given independent sets of equal size can be transformed into the other by moving one token at a time while keeping the occupied vertices independent. In token sliding, a token moves along an edge. In token jumping, it may move to any unoccupied vertex. For both rules, the problem is solvable in polynomial time on trees and is PSPACE-complete on graphs of treewidth at most $c$ for some fixed constant $c$. For each rule, the smallest treewidth bound that suffices for hardness has long been open. We narrow this gap by proving that both versions are NP-hard on graphs of treewidth four.

2611.20136.title: An isolated complex Hadamard matrix with nonzero defect
2611.20136.abstract: We exhibit a complex Hadamard matrix of nonzero defect which is isolated among complex Hadamard matrices, up to Hadamard equivalence. This counterexample is realized by a Butson-type Hadamard matrix of size $13$, with entries roots of order $6$ of unity. In the language of commuting squares, this shows that the span condition, previously introduced by the second author as a sufficient condition for isolation, is not a necessary condition for isolation.

2611.20133.title: Robust Antiferromagnetic Ordering above 500 K in a Family of Bilayer van der Waals Materials
2611.20133.abstract: Stabilizing magnetic order above room temperature in layered materials is highly desirable for low-dimensional spintronics applications. However, realizing room-temperature antiferromagnetism in layered magnets remains challenging. Here, we present a layered semiconducting oxyhalide material family, Sr$_3$Fe$_2$O$_5$X$_2$ ($X$ = F, Cl, Br), which exhibits robust high-temperature antiferromagnetic ordering. The two-dimensional nature and scalability of this system are demonstrated by atomically resolving the van der Waals gap of Sr$_3$Fe$_2$O$_5$Br$_2$ and synthesizing centimeter-scale single crystals of Sr$_3$Fe$_2$O$_5$Cl$_2$. Temperature-dependent neutron scattering and magnetization measurements determine their G-type magnetic structure and transition temperature. Remarkably, the Néel temperature of Sr$_3$Fe$_2$O$_5$F$_2$ ($\sim$580 K) is the highest among all reported layered antiferromagnets. Density functional theory calculations demonstrate that strong nearest-neighbor superexchange interactions along both out-of-plane and in-plane directions, particularly the magnetic couplings along lattice $c$ direction within the bilayer motif, are primarily responsible for the high Néel temperatures in Sr$_3$Fe$_2$O$_5$X$_2$. In contrast, inter-bilayer spin couplings are negligibly weak, without much influence on the stabilization of the antiferromagnetic order. Therefore, theoretical calculations predict that this robust antiferromagnetic order could persist or even strengthens at room-temperature even at the monolayer limit. Our results highlight iron-based layered oxyhalides as a promising platform for exploring beyond-room-temperature antiferromagnetism in the two-dimensional limit, holding immense potential in areas like information storage and spin-based devices.
2611.20133.comment: Accepted for publication at SCIENCE CHINA Physics, Mechanics & Astronomy

2611.22357.title: Topological Timing of Bound States by Spacetime Mass Windings
2611.22357.abstract: Topology usually determines where a wave is trapped. Here we show that it can also determine when a trapped state brightens or dims. We consider a dimerized photonic lattice in which a real Dirac mass, varying in space, binds a Jackiw-Rebbi state, while staggered gain and loss, switched in time, act as an imaginary Dirac mass on that same state. Together, the two masses form a mass field in space and time whose isolated zeros carry an integer winding. Combining a continuum Dirac description with finite-lattice simulations, we show that the sign of this winding fixes whether the bound state reaches a maximum or a minimum at the switch, while the gain and loss remain below the bulk gap. The windings obey a conservation law: they are created and annihilated in pairs, and their sum along a boundary determines which extrema are protected. Full-wave simulations of a passive waveguide array, in which the propagation distance plays the role of time, reproduce these predictions with loss alone. These results provide a topological handle on the timing of localized optical responses, relevant to switching, gating, and pulse shaping of confined modes in integrated photonic circuits and topological lasers.

2611.22662.title: Domain walls of a spin-chirality ferroelectric as tunable quantum particles
2611.22662.abstract: In frustrated spin chains with competing nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor exchange, the vector spin chirality sets the electric polarization, so a ferroelectric domain wall is a domain wall of the chirality. The semiclassical picture suggests nonlocal switching dynamics due to topological constraints on the spins, but little is known about such domain walls in a quantum spin chain. Using density-matrix renormalization group calculations for a frustrated spin-1/2 XXZ chain in which a bond alternation $δ$ opens a spin gap, we show that the wall then becomes a quantum particle. In a finite chain, it has the energy levels and wave functions of a particle in a box, and it moves under an electric field as a particle under a constant force does. In the infinite chain, its mass grows by more than two orders of magnitude as $δ$ decreases and diverges at $δ^*\approx0.012$, where the bottom of its band becomes flat; below $δ^*$ the band has two degenerate minima away from its center. The large mass results from a near cancellation of in-plane and out-of-plane exchange energies.

2611.22573.title: Targeted material doping to enable the formation and coherent propagation of Laser Induced Periodic Surface Structures (LIPSS): the ZnO paradigm
2611.22573.abstract: This work explores how the initial free carrier density governs the formation and coherent propagation of Low Spatial Frequency Laser-Induced Periodic Surface Structures (LSF-LIPSS). As a paradigm we have analyzed the behavior of ad-hoc-doped ZnO films. ZnO is a multifunctional Transparent Conducting Oxide (TCO) with many scientific and technologic uses including applications in biomedicine, photonics, sensing or photocatalysis. Many of them would benefit from the use of large area, electrically anisotropic surfaces. By introducing small amounts of Yb3+ as donor dopant in ZnO films grown by Pulse Laser Deposition (PLD), we have substantially improved its carrier density at room temperature (RT) and its electrical conductivity while preserving the functional properties of pure ZnO. For RT carrier densities ne > 1019 cm-3, coherent propagation of LSF-LIPSS has been successfully achieved upon irradiation with 350 fs laser pulses at 1030 nm at high repetition rate (500 kHz) and for laser scanning speeds well above 1 m/s. However, the ablation mechanism (ZnO sublimation at the LIPSS valleys) and the large melting temperature of ZnO, make the thermal conductivity of the substrate, the film thickness and the irradiation pulse duration to play a crucial role in determining the morphology of the LSF-LIPPS propagated over large areas, especially in avoiding film cracking. The results achieved upon optimization fully confirm the role of free carrier density in the large-scale propagation of high quality LSF-LIPSS in doped ZnO and enable using these structures to easily generate large electrical anisotropies over macroscopic regions with conductivities along the LIPSS several times larger than transversally.

2611.22694.title: Thermal and Acoustic Measurements of Hybrid Bonding Stacks
2611.22694.abstract: Thermal and structural characterizations of hybrid bonding structures are essential for understanding heat transport in three-dimensional integrated circuits (3D-ICs). In this work, we investigate the effective thermal conductivity of the Cu/dielectric HB layer using time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) combined with picosecond ultrasonic technique. Shallow-angle polishing enabled depth-resolved thermal measurements by exposing hybrid bonding layers with different remaining thicknesses, while acoustic echoes were used to identify buried interfaces and determine the thickness. The distinct waveform of the bonding interface echo compared with the Cu/dielectric interface echo suggests that its acoustic response may also reflect the interfacial bonding conditions. The extracted thermal conductivity ranges from 1.14 to 1.75 Wm-1K-1 for the bottom pad layer and from 1.76 to 4.34 Wm-1K-1 for the top pad layer. The difference in thermal conductivity is consistent with the different Cu area fractions of the two layers. Furthermore, the thermal conductivity of the top pad layer increases significantly with the remaining thickness, possibly due to the thermal boundary resistance at the bonding interface, low thermal conductivity of SiCN interlayer, and increased electron scattering in thin Cu structures. Our work demonstrates a practical approach to investigate the thermal properties of buried hybrid bonding layers, providing experimental data for thermal design and modeling of 3D-ICs.

2611.22529.title: Solvent/Antisolvent-Driven Etching of 2D Layered Halide Perovskite Microcrystals toward Endo-Epitaxial Heterostructures
2611.22529.abstract: Engineering internal interfaces within single crystals remains challenging, particularly in soft ionic materials such as layered halide perovskites (LHPs), for which conventional lithographic approaches are difficult to implement. Here we report a solvent/antisolvent-driven strategy for controlled etching of LHP microcrystals, producing well-defined rectangular cavities. Etching initiates at the top surface and proceeds preferentially along the crystallographic [100] and [010] directions. Cavity dimensions are tuned through etching time, temperature and etchant composition. The reaction can be interrupted and resumed, enabling stepwise cavity evolution through successive etching cycles. The resulting cavities serve as confined templates for regrowth of compositionally distinct LHPs, yielding endo-epitaxial heterostructures with designed internal architectures. The approach extends across diverse LHP compositions and antisolvent systems, while sequential precursor addition controls the extent of internal regrowth. This strategy establishes a route to engineering internal heterointerfaces in single-crystal perovskites through controlled chemical etching and confined growth.

2611.22690.title: The minimum degree of minimally k-extendable graphs for some k
2611.22690.abstract: A graph on at least 2k+2 vertices is k-extendable if every matching of size k extends to a perfect matching, and it is minimally k-extendable if it is k-extendable but deleting any edge is not. Plummer proved that every k-extendable graph is (k+1)-connected. So its minimum degree is at least k+1. Lou and Yu conjectured that a minimally k-extendable graph on at most 4k vertices has minimum degree in {k+1,2k,2k+1}; the case k=1 and the claw-free case of k=2 have been settled previously. We determine the minimum degree of minimally k-extendable graphs for k=2 and k=3, thereby settling the Lou--Yu conjecture for these two values. For k=2 the minimum degree is in {3,4,5}. For k=3 it is in {4,7} at orders 8 and 10, and in {4,6,7} at order 12. The proofs pass to the complement graph and combine Tutte's perfect matching theorem with a classification of four-vertex and six-vertex obstructions. All predicted values are realized by explicit constructions.
2611.22690.comment: 12 pages, 1 figure. Submitted to Graphs and Combinatorics

2611.22656.title: Golomb rulers with real marks: the real and integer optima agree up to ten marks
2611.22656.abstract: A Golomb ruler is a set of integer marks whose pairwise differences are distinct. We let the marks be real numbers and ask that every difference be at least 1 and that any two differences be at least 1 apart. Every integer Golomb ruler satisfies these conditions, so the least length $G_R(n)$ of such a real ruler with $n$ marks is at most the optimal Golomb length $G_Z(n)$. Fixing the order of all differences splits the real problem into finitely many polyhedral chambers. A branch-and-bound over these chambers, with an exact rational certificate at every leaf, proves $G_R(n) = G_Z(n)$ for $n \le 10$. Each proof takes under a minute and is verified by an independent checker that uses only exact arithmetic. An exhaustive exact enumeration of all chamber vertices confirms the result for $n \le 7$, and shows that there the shortest real rulers are exactly the optimal integer rulers and their mirror images. For every $n$ we show $n(\sqrt{n}-1)^2 \le G_R(n) \le G_Z(n)$, so that $G_R(n) \sim G_Z(n) \sim n^2$. Non-integral chamber vertices first appear at $n = 7$: there are 84, all half-integral. Already there, 80 of them are shortest points of their chambers, 40 of them the only one, although the global optimum is integral; a twelve-mark example of the same kind comes from Singer's construction. On the other hand, every Singer ruler with at most 104 marks, cut at the largest gap, is the only shortest point of its own chamber; we conjecture this for all prime powers.
2611.22656.comment: 9 pages, 5 tables. Programs, proof files and exact checkers: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23843508

2611.22440.title: The shape of individual differences in judgment: shared axes, personal weights, and when their spread crosses the consensus
2611.22440.abstract: People differ in how they judge faces, artworks, photographs and jokes. Previous work measured the size of these differences; we ask what shape they take. We wrote three candidate shapes as nested generative models (same-sign reweighting of shared dimensions, a linear transform that allows reversal, and stimulus-specific offsets) and compared how well they predict people unseen in training, using ten public datasets (about 20,000 raters). The models recovered a person's judgment space from 10-20 judgments and predicted judgments of unseen stimuli. For faces, reweighting was sufficient, and weights opposing the population were not statistically detected. For artworks, weights spread continuously along the shared abstract-figurative direction, and 28 percent of raters fell on the opposite side from the population. This tail was much smaller when a different rater sample judged the same artworks. Individual differences thus differ in shape as well as size, and the shape depends on domain and raters.

2611.22507.title: A sharp minimum degree condition for Hamiltonicity in line graphs of 3-hypergraphs
2611.22507.abstract: Let $G$ be the line graph of a $3$-hypergraph, and let $n$ be its order. We prove that if $G$ is $3$-connected, $n\ge4936$, and $δ(G)\ge(n+5)/10$, then $G$ is Hamiltonian if and only if it does not belong to an explicitly described family of exceptional graphs. This extends the sharp minimum degree bound of Lai, Shao, and Zhan for $3$-connected claw-free graphs beyond the claw-free setting, since line graphs of $3$-hypergraphs may contain induced claws. The coefficient $1/10$ cannot be decreased, and the constant $5$ in the numerator cannot be replaced by $4$.

2611.22483.title: Manufacturing Differential Sparsity: Planner-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient World Model Planning
2611.22483.abstract: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward new goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.

2611.22070.title: Why do continual physical learners need sleep?
2611.22070.abstract: Sleep is widespread across the animal kingdom, including in organisms without a centralized nervous system. Does learning create a need for sleep, even without biology? To explore this question, we study a disordered spring network trained to perform a sequence of mechanical allosteric tasks through local changes in bond stiffness. We find that continual learning progressively reduces the network's ability to acquire new tasks as individual bonds become increasingly specialized. We identify an exact algebraic relationship between the polarization of bond dominance and the network's remaining learning capacity, providing a quantitative measure of this loss of adaptability.
